name: Database Sharding
intent: Split one large database into several smaller ones (shards), each holding part of the data, so storage and write load are spread across machines.
scenario: A social app has 100 million users. One database server can no longer store them all or keep up with the writes, even on the biggest machine available.
problem: Replicas can multiply read capacity, but every replica still holds all the data and every write still goes to one primary. When the data no longer fits on one machine, or writes saturate it, scaling up is exhausted and replication does not help. The data itself has to be divided.

howItWorks.title: Choose a shard key
howItWorks.text: Pick the column that decides where a row lives, for example user_id. A good key spreads data and traffic evenly and appears in most queries. This is the most important and hardest-to-change decision.

howItWorks.title: Route each request to a shard
howItWorks.text: Hash sharding computes hash(key) mod N, which spreads keys evenly. Range sharding assigns key ranges to shards, which keeps neighbours together and supports range scans. A directory (lookup table) can place keys anywhere, at the cost of one more service.

howItWorks.title: Queries by key touch one shard
howItWorks.text: Fetching user 42 goes straight to the shard that owns it. Queries that do not include the key must ask every shard and merge the results (scatter-gather), which is slower and costs more.

howItWorks.title: Resharding is painful
howItWorks.text: With plain modulo, changing N from 3 to 4 moves about three quarters of all keys. Consistent hashing or many small virtual shards limit the movement to roughly 1/N.

howItWorks.title: Watch for hot shards
howItWorks.text: Skewed keys, a celebrity user, or sequential ids with range sharding can send most traffic to one shard while the others idle. Each shard should usually also be replicated for availability.

pros: Capacity for data and writes grows by adding shards
Each shard is smaller, so queries and indexes are faster
A failure affects only part of the data
Can place data near the users who own it
cons: Cross-shard queries, joins and transactions become hard or impossible
Resharding and rebalancing are complex and risky
Hot shards if the key is chosen badly
Much more operational work: routing, migrations, backups, schema changes per shard
whenToUse: The data or write rate has outgrown the largest practical single database
Most queries can be answered with the shard key
You have already used caching, indexing and read replicas
whenNotToUse: The database fits comfortably on one machine with headroom
Your queries are mostly joins and reports across all the data
You need strong multi-row transactions across the whole dataset
Early on: sharding too soon adds cost without benefit
pitfalls: Choosing a shard key with low cardinality or skew, such as country
Using sequential ids with range sharding, so every new row hits the last shard
Using modulo hashing and then discovering how much data a new shard moves
Application code that quietly assumes a single database, such as cross-table joins
